title: Predictive laws linking erosion, sediment transport and landscape evolution

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a physically grounded framework that predicts how rock is worn away, how the resulting sediment moves, and how these processes reshape channels and landscapes. It would connect measurable properties of rock, sediment supply and flowing water to landscape change, while specifying uncertainty and the conditions under which each prediction applies. Extending those connections to ice flow, climate variability and tectonic forcing across event and geological timescales is part of the broader research objective; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate that full capability.

A central physical complication is that sediment can both cause erosion and prevent it. Moving particles can strike and abrade exposed bedrock, while sediment covering the bed can shield it from impacts. Changes in sediment supply and flow conditions can therefore change the erosion regime. The supplied study identifies extreme sediment-rich flows as processes that need better integration into longer-term bedrock-channel models.

Proposed scope: success need not take the form of one equation for every landscape. A connected set of regime-dependent laws could provide the advance if it reliably identifies which processes dominate, predicts transitions between regimes and carries uncertainty through to landscape-scale outcomes. Historical reconstruction would be a related task: determining which past conditions the observed landscape actually constrains, rather than assuming that a good forward model automatically identifies one unique history.

significance.text: The revolutionary step would be predictive transfer across settings and timescales: using physical understanding to anticipate erosion, sediment movement and landform change beyond the sites used to develop a model. The supplied study illustrates why this matters. Long-term channel development may reflect alternating periods of little erosion and brief episodes of intense erosion, so measurements of ordinary conditions alone may give an incomplete account of how a landscape formed.

Conditional consequence: better forward predictions could make landforms a more reliable quantitative record of past climate and tectonic forcing. Researchers could compare competing histories by testing whether they produce the observed landscape under physically credible conditions. This would strengthen inference, but would not by itself guarantee a unique reconstruction. Independent geological, chronological or climatic constraints would still be needed to distinguish histories that remain compatible with the observations. The supplied article discusses competing explanations for gorge formation; it does not establish general mathematical nonuniqueness of landscape histories.

Conditional downstream possibility: a validated framework could improve forecasts of erosion and sediment movement relevant to natural hazards. Operational benefit would depend on knowing the relevant rock and sediment properties, water or ice forcing, boundary conditions and probabilities of extreme events. Predicting landscape response to a specified event is a different capability from predicting when that event will occur or which particular disaster will happen. No operational forecasting benefit, numerical impact estimate or likelihood of achieving the broader framework is demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a validated connection between local erosion mechanisms and larger-scale landscape evolution under changing conditions. The 2024 article describes existing process laws and landscape models, but identifies limitations in models that do not directly represent physical channel-erosion processes and in applying a single fluvial-incision theory across different climates and sediment supplies. A stronger framework would need to represent sediment's erosive and shielding effects and explain when different transport and erosion regimes apply.

A concrete barrier is connecting short, powerful events to geological averages. Extreme sediment-rich flows may substantially alter bedrock within a brief interval, yet their cumulative contribution depends on recurrence, sediment availability, water supply and intervening periods of weak or absent erosion. The supplied paper argues for including such events in landscape evolution models; its single-event measurements do not establish their general long-term contribution.

Measurement also constrains model development. In the documented gorge, occlusion, restricted underwater coverage and an approximately 2 cm detection limit left parts of the erosion unmeasured or undetected. Direct analysis of channel-bed incision was omitted. These limitations make it difficult to infer complete erosion from observed surface changes and reinforce the need to distinguish measured lateral erosion from total channel change.

Broader proposed challenges include coupling river and ice erosion to tectonic forcing, transferring laws between contrasting geological settings, and determining when historical reconstructions are identifiable from available observations. These remain requirements of this concept, rather than capabilities established or comprehensively assessed by the supplied channel study. Competing explanations for one gorge's development motivate reconstruction tests but do not prove that different histories necessarily produce indistinguishable landscapes throughout the proposed scope.

current_state.text: The supplied dated evidence is the study “Hyperconcentrated flows shape bedrock channels” by Verena Stammberger, Benjamin Jacobs and Michael Krautblatter, published in Communications Earth & Environment on 8 April 2024. It describes existing erosion laws and landscape models while identifying incomplete integration of extreme sediment-rich flows into longer-term bedrock-channel models. This is evidence of the study's contemporary assessment, rather than a comprehensive assessment of the field in November 2026.

For a hyperconcentrated flow on 13 June 2020 in a limestone gorge, pre-event and post-event LiDAR surveys documented substantial lateral erosion of bedrock walls during an event lasting about one hour. The reported detected lateral erosion volume was 20.60 cubic metres, with channel-averaged lateral erosion of 3.41 mm. These are measured results from a particular event and setting; they do not establish transferable predictions across landscapes or geological timescales.

The measurement scope matters. The researchers omitted direct analysis of bed incision and focused on lateral bedrock-wall erosion because of coverage limitations. Occlusion, restricted underwater observations and an approximately 2 cm detection limit made the detected changes conservative and incomplete measures of total erosion. The channel-averaged 3.41 mm value should therefore not be interpreted as a measurement of vertical incision or as evidence that all millimetre-scale surface changes were resolved.

The authors interpret extreme sediment-rich events as potentially important contributors to longer-term gorge development. Their discussion also emphasizes that present conditions may not supply enough sediment or water to reproduce effective erosion frequently. That interpretation motivates integration into landscape models, but it remains distinct from directly measuring long-term incision or validating a general reconstruction framework.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review reports an identity-verified, untruncated text extraction spanning all 15 article pages. Figure images and supplementary material were not inspected, although the event findings and measurement restrictions were explicitly reported in the extracted results and methods. The supplied freshness search record is empty, so it does not establish whether the broader integration gap remained open on 1 November 2026. That limitation does not invalidate the dated observations or show that later progress did not occur.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: develop a physically grounded framework with explicit regimes, required inputs, limits of applicability and uncertainty estimates, then predict withheld erosion rates, sediment fluxes and landform changes across contrasting settings. Predictions should be recorded before the withheld observations are used for tuning. A validated family of laws would qualify if the framework also explains how to select and connect them; a single universal equation is not required.
completion_criteria.label: Framework predicts withheld erosion rates, sediment fluxes and landform changes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed timescale test: evaluate both ordinary conditions and rare, sediment-rich events, then test whether their combined contributions explain longer-term change. Measurements should distinguish lateral erosion, bed incision, sediment storage and sediment export wherever those quantities are part of the prediction. Where coverage or detection limits prevent complete observations, the comparison should explicitly retain those limits instead of treating detected change as the whole response. The source motivates event inclusion and measurement discipline, but does not prescribe this completion protocol.
completion_criteria.label: Ordinary conditions and rare sediment-rich events jointly explain longer-term change

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and transfer test: independent groups should be able to reproduce the predictions using documented observations, methods and model implementations, then evaluate them in locations and regimes outside the original calibration set. Claimed coverage of ice erosion or tectonic forcing would require corresponding demonstrations. Evaluation should report where predictions fail, where inputs are insufficient and how uncertainty behaves. These are proposed criteria, not established community thresholds; finite tests demonstrate breadth within tested conditions, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent groups reproduce predictions and test transfer beyond calibration regimes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed historical-inference test: use cases with independent constraints on past conditions to assess whether the framework recovers those constraints or correctly retains multiple plausible histories. A convincing result would distinguish information supplied by the landscape from information supplied by external evidence. Practical success would include recognizing when a reconstruction or hazard forecast is insufficiently constrained, rather than always producing a precise answer.
completion_criteria.label: Historical inference recovers independent constraints or retains multiple plausible histories

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison and synthesis: GEO-01, “Reliable short-term forecasting of damaging earthquakes,” and GEO-10, “Reliable transferable forecasting of volcanic eruptions,” share the goal of physically informed predictions with explicit uncertainty and validation outside the development setting. GEO-09 concerns erosion, sediment transport and landscape response. Predicting those responses to an earthquake or eruption would not establish the ability to forecast either triggering event.

Roster comparison and synthesis: GEO-08, “Establishing when and how sustained plate tectonics began,” overlaps through tectonic forcing and interpretation of geological records. GEO-05, “Recovery of a detailed geological record of Earth’s first half-billion years,” and GEO-07, “Reconstructing the Moon-forming impact from independent geological evidence,” also concern inference from surviving evidence. GEO-09 could inform how erosion modifies or removes records, but it would not itself recover missing early-Earth evidence, date the onset of sustained plate tectonics or reconstruct the Moon-forming impact.

Roster comparison and synthesis: GEO-02, “A chemically and thermally resolved map of Earth’s deep interior,” concerns subsurface structure rather than surface transport and landform evolution. Deep-Earth processes can enter GEO-09 as broader geological forcing, but a validated erosion framework would not provide that interior map. Conversely, interior mapping alone would not resolve sediment shielding, event-driven erosion or channel evolution.

Roster comparison and synthesis: GEO-03, “Geothermal reservoirs engineered economically in ordinary deep rock,” GEO-04, “Global-scale, verifiable mineral storage of carbon dioxide,” and GEO-06, “Discovery of globally consequential recoverable geological hydrogen,” share attention to rock properties and geological setting. Their central advances concern engineered reservoirs, carbon storage and recoverable resources, respectively. Landscape predictions could provide site context or help assess surface change, but would not demonstrate reservoir economics, storage verification or recoverable hydrogen at consequential scale.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the state of broader landscape-model integration on 1 November 2026 or document subsequent advances beyond the 2024 study.
Transferability across rock types, glacial settings, tectonic regimes and event-to-geological timescales remains unestablished by the supplied single-gorge evidence.
The frequency and cumulative long-term contribution of events like the June 2020 flow are not established by its measured lateral erosion.
Total event erosion, including channel-bed incision and changes outside survey coverage or below the detection limit, is not resolved by the reported measurements.
General conditions for unique or nonunique landscape-history reconstruction are not established; competing gorge explanations alone do not resolve that question.
Figure images and supplementary material were not inspected in the supplied review, so their additional evidence or qualifications remain outside this record.
No quantitative acceptance thresholds or historical calibration demonstrations were supplied for the broader proposed framework.

brief.title: Predictions of how water and ice reshape the land
possible: Researchers could predict how rivers wear away rock, move sediment—the loose material erosion produces—and reshape valleys under changing conditions. The predictions would work beyond the places used to develop them, with clear estimates of uncertainty.

They could test competing explanations of how a landscape formed and forecast its response to a specified extreme event. The broader goal includes changes driven by ice, climate and movements of Earth’s crust.
why: A landscape can change through long quiet periods punctuated by brief, intense erosion. Connecting both would help researchers explain how valleys develop and use their shapes to learn about past climate and movements of Earth’s crust.
Better predictions of erosion and sediment movement could also improve forecasts relevant to natural hazards.

shown: Researchers have measured substantial wall erosion during a brief sediment-rich flow, linked river measurements to longer-term erosion, and compared simulated sediment movement with reservoir deposits. These are separate demonstrations in particular settings.

Stammberger and colleagues directly observed an extreme flow’s effects in a limestone gorge. Their measurements covered wall erosion; they did not directly measure how far the channel floor was cut down.
missing: Connected physical laws must predict when moving sediment wears rock away and when sediment cover protects it.
Ordinary flows and rare events must together account for long-term change, including erosion and sediment stored or carried away.
Predictions must work across contrasting rocks, river and ice settings, and timescales, with uncertainty carried through.
Tests must establish what past conditions landscapes can reveal and when several histories remain plausible.

milestones.label: Predictions succeed against observations withheld from model development
milestones.explanation: A framework would have to predict erosion rates, sediment movement and landform change across contrasting settings, with clear conditions and uncertainty. This would test its ability to predict beyond examples used to develop it.

milestones.label: Ordinary flows and rare events explain long-term change
milestones.explanation: Their combined effects would have to explain longer-term change, distinguishing wall and bed erosion from sediment storage and export while retaining measurement limits. This would connect brief events to landscape development.

milestones.label: Independent groups reproduce predictions and test new settings
milestones.explanation: Independent groups would have to reproduce predictions and test settings beyond those used to tune the model, including any claimed ice or crustal effects. This would establish its tested reach, failures and uncertainty.

milestones.label: Landscape histories recover independent evidence or preserve alternatives
milestones.explanation: Reconstructions would have to recover independently known past conditions or retain several plausible histories, separating landscape clues from external evidence. This would test when historical answers are justified.

uncertain: How often do extreme sediment-rich flows occur, and how much long-term erosion do they account for?
Under what conditions can a landscape distinguish between competing histories?
What prediction accuracy and uncertainty would count as success across the proposed settings and timescales?

page.title: Geomorphic transport laws for landscape evolution
page.definition: A connected set of physical laws would predict rock erosion, sediment flux—the amount of loose material transported per unit time—and landform change from measured forcing and material properties. The laws would transfer beyond calibration settings, from individual events to geological timescales.

goal.need: In one 900 m limestone gorge, surveys detected 232 erosion patches from a sediment-rich flow on 13 June 2020. Direct analysis of bed incision was omitted. Connecting these event measurements to sediment budgets and long-term landscape change requires distinguishing erosion mechanisms and sediment cover; the study calls for including sediment-rich extremes in long-term models.

figures.caption: Measured effects of one hyperconcentrated flow in the Höllental gorge
figures.note: These are conservative wall-erosion measurements. They exclude direct analysis of channel-bed incision.

statements.quote: To tackle this challenge we need to discover, quantify, test, and apply mathematical laws that define the rates of processes shaping Earth’s surface.
statements.context: The challenge is identifying the transport laws governing Earth's surface evolution.

completion.title: Transport laws predict erosion, sediment flux and landform change beyond their calibration settings.
completion.criterion: A connected set of mechanistic transport laws predicts erosion rates, sediment fluxes and topographic change in independent landscapes, without fitting parameters to the observations being predicted. Tests cover changing sediment supply and forcing, including ordinary flows and sediment-rich extremes, from individual events to geological timescales. Predicted and observed responses agree within independently constrained observational and predictive uncertainty. Applicability limits and regime transitions are tested. No universal numerical tolerance has been published for this combined test.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback, informed by the NRC research challenges and CSDMS programme goals; no external combined acceptance test was found.
completion.basis: Searched the NRC's 2010 research challenges, CSDMS's 2004 implementation plan and 2024 strategy, transport-law definitions, independent-watershed validation studies, and watershed-model performance guidelines for a combined acceptance test; none was found. These sources call for testable process laws and prediction across scales. Monthly sediment criteria do not certify bedrock erosion or geological topography. This fallback connects those goals without assigning a universal error percentage.

milestones.title: A mechanistic erosion law reproduces laboratory responses to sediment supply and grain size.
milestones.criterion: A mechanistic erosion or transport law reproduces the response to controlled experimental changes, with identifiable physical parameters. Dietrich et al. require physical-model testability, without specifying an error cutoff. Sklar and Dietrich (2004) used six 100-impact drop tests on two artificial sandstones, from 1.0 m, to constrain wear resistance, and compared modelled abrasion with abrasion-mill measurements as grain size and sediment supply varied. This establishes laboratory support for one erosion mechanism.
milestones.set_by: Physical-model testing convention described by Dietrich et al. in the 2003 AGU monograph; applied to bedrock abrasion by Sklar and Dietrich in 2004.
milestones.threshold_quote: can be tested in physical models

milestones.title: Field measurements parameterize a geomorphic transport law.
milestones.criterion: The law's parameters are constrained by field measurements of process rates and their controls. This follows Dietrich et al.'s field-parameterization condition; it sets no numerical accuracy cutoff. Collins et al. (2016) measured three channel-bed transects during 1999–2003 in one 102 km² catchment. Several-year erosion resembled the century-scale rate inferred from the lowest strath terrace, an abandoned bedrock channel surface. These are supporting mechanism and rate observations, rather than validation of a transferable law.
milestones.set_by: Field-parameterization condition in Dietrich et al.'s 2003 definition of geomorphic transport laws.
milestones.threshold_quote: can be parameterized from field measurements

milestones.title: Watershed sediment predictions reach monthly R² > 0.40, NSE > 0.45 and absolute bias ≤20%.
milestones.criterion: For watershed sediment simulations, monthly R² > 0.40 and Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) > 0.45, with absolute percent bias ≤20% at daily, monthly or annual resolution. R² measures linear association; NSE compares squared prediction errors with an observed-mean predictor. The authors caution against unqualified use beyond the reviewed models. Gioia and Lazzari (2019), one approximately 9 km² catchment, reported 4,288 m³/year over 18 simulated years, approximately 20% below reservoir estimates. Monthly R² and NSE were not reported, so passage is unestablished.
milestones.set_by: Moriasi et al., 2015 watershed-model evaluation guidelines, published in Transactions of the ASABE. The sediment recommendations principally concern SWAT, HSPF and WARMF; application to other models requires caution.
milestones.threshold_quote: monthly R2 > 0.40 and NSE > 0.45 and daily, monthly, or annual PBIAS ≤±20% for sediment

milestones.title: A landscape model retains its improvement over a base model in an independent watershed.
milestones.criterion: Model improvements identified in calibration persist when the calibrated models are applied to an independent watershed and compared using the same topographic objective function. Barnhart et al. (2020) tested 34 calibrated models on five initial topographies over 13,000 years; one initial-topography alternative was excluded from further analysis. Distinguishing bedrock from glacial till remained beneficial, but the calibration winner lost its clear advantage over other rock–till models. This supports relative model choices in a similar watershed, without establishing joint prediction of erosion, sediment flux and topography across regimes.
milestones.set_by: Independent-validation convention applied by Barnhart et al., 2020, sections 3.4 and 5.2. The published application concerns two similar watersheds.
milestones.threshold_quote: Validation tests which model improvements persist when models are applied to an independent watershed.

not_found: The supplied TUM and CNR PDF links could not be retrieved; publisher and author-posted copies were accessible.
No joint independent validation spanning event erosion, sediment flux and geological topographic change across contrasting regimes was located.

results.finding: One gorge experienced 3.41 mm mean lateral erosion during a single hyperconcentrated flow.
results.detail: Field measurements document erosion and its relationship to channel geometry, but the study does not use them to constrain parameters of a geomorphic transport law. The estimate is a conservative minimum.
results.quote:
The mean erosion of the sections with
detected erosion is 4.89 mm (median 1.69 mm) and 3.41 mm (median
0.76 mm) for the whole channel including the areas with no detected ero-
sion.

results.finding: High-flow incision correlated positively with peak annual flow at 2 transects.
results.detail: Field measurements link incision rates to a potential control, but the paper does not use them to constrain parameters of a geomorphic transport law.
results.quote:
At the two more rapidly incising transects 
(cross-sections 2 and 4), annual incision in the 
high-flow channel correlates positively with 
peak annual flow (Fig. 10).

results.finding: In one catchment, simulated erosion averaged 4,288 m³/year, about 20% below reservoir sedimentation.
results.detail: The comparison used an approximately 18-year aggregate. Monthly R² and NSE were not reported, so the criterion is not established. The rainfall and reservoir observation periods also differed.
results.quote:
The model provided a reasonable
estimation of erosion processes of 4288 m 3 year−1, which is about 20% lower than the estimated
annual sedimentation volumes from the bathymetric survey.

results.finding: A total-load abrasion model fit 29 tabulated erosion measurements across grain sizes when impacts below St = 75 were damped.
results.detail: The experiments varied grain size while holding sediment load and flow speed fixed; sediment-supply changes were modeled but not tested. The substrate was polyurethane foam. Some experiment identifiers in the table are repeated.
results.quote:

sion model where impacts are viscously damped 
for St < 75; this value is within the range of par-
tial dampening found in particle-wall collision 
studies (e.g., Joseph et al., 2001).

results.finding: A physical bedload flux model matched a compilation of experiments and simulations within a factor of 1.3; total sample size not stated.
results.detail: The model has identifiable physical parameters and was tested across grain shapes and flow conditions. The provided text does not establish a test of its response to controlled changes in sediment supply and grain size.

results.finding: Across 3 field sites, a depth-dependent soil transport law was fitted; Nunnock River’s transport coefficient was 0.55 cm yr⁻¹.
results.detail: Flux was inferred from soil production rates and field measurements of soil depth and slope, assuming negligible soil-storage change. The depth-slope relationship did not fit Point Reyes; possible spurious covariance and nonconstant transport coefficients limit interpretation.

results.finding: In one Bayin River watershed, modified SWAT achieved monthly sediment-yield validation R² of 0.87.
results.detail: For 2017–2018 validation, monthly NSE was 0.86 and PBIAS was −15.20%. Calibration PBIAS was 21.24%, outside the criterion’s 20% limit.
